claim.description: A proposition, including proposals, user-stated positions and challenged formulations; status records its standing.

question.description: An unresolved or answered inquiry; answers are linked claims.

case.description: An experience or case-study summary, with source provenance.

source.description: A source artifact or provenance context.

entity.description: A named domain role or object type that statements refer to; subtype is recorded in metadata.

operation.description: A named action whose meaning is distinct from its permission or implementation.

trace.description: An explicitly bounded event trace extracted from evidence or constructed as a synthetic fixture. Roles are recorded at event time.

check-result.description: A reproducible bounded pattern evaluation tied to exact claim and trace inputs; not a proof of the prose theory.

supports.description: Source supplies a reason to believe the target claim; not a proof.

answers.description: Claim offers full, partial or unknown coverage of a question. Only a current accepted full answer resolves it; partial answers preserve the remainder.

challenges.description: Source disputes or supplies a potential counterexample to the target claim.

revises.description: Source updates or corrects the target earlier formulation.

motivates.description: Source explains why the target question is worth asking; does not answer it.

informs.description: Source contributes context for the target proposal without logical entailment.

raises.description: Source gives rise to the target unresolved question.

about.description: Source claim, question or evidence concerns the target domain anchor; no assertion of truth or implication.

governs.description: Source claim specifies a responsibility, permission or constraint concerning the target operation; conditions remain in the claim text.

potential-conflict.description: Recorded possible incompatibility between claims requiring interpretation of conditions and scope. Not proof of contradiction.

checks.description: A saved computation checked this input; does not imply support or acceptance.

depends-on.description: Dependent question or claim → mandatory prerequisite. The dependent is not ready until the prerequisite is answered or accepted. Use only for a real dependency.

acts-on.description: Operation → the entity it reads or changes. Lets a reader walk from an entity to the operations on it.

extracted-from.description: Interpretation was extracted from the source. Source fingerprints bind saved evidence; the source needs no accepted standing.

performed-by.description: Operation → the role that performs it. Lets a reader walk from a role to what it does.

agent-definition.text: Candidate: A = (R, C, U, J), accompanied by a running policy P = (start, drive). This separates what an agent owes, what it reads, what it can do and how it judges, from what launches it and permits its next turn. This is a candidate construction, not a ratified definition.

dials-configure-steward.text: The steward's autonomy is bounded by dials: operator-authored sentences, each with a weight from 0 to 10, saying what should reach the operator and what the steward may handle itself. The steward weighs an intention against them and either files work directly or sends the intention to the operator. The set of dials is open; the operator adds, rewords and reweights them.

desk-is-operator-list.text: The desk is the operator's list of items on which the operator owes the next action. It is an interface, not an agent and not a contract node. file-intention.text: Bring a new intention into existence. The front door: anyone outside, or any agent, may file. A filed, unprocessed intention wakes the steward.

reassess-intention.text: The steward claims an intention and reads all prior work against it, then chooses: more work, wait, send to the desk, or settle. Triggered by rest of a linked record or a new filing.

send-to-desk.text: Put an item on the operator's desk with a trace of why. Not steward-only: the steward sends intentions the dials say the operator must see; the orchestrator sends execution questions directly. While the item is on the desk the operator owes the next action.

answer-at-desk.text: The operator answers an item on the desk, at the desk or in an agent thread. The answer is recorded against the durable item and ownership of the next action returns to the sender.

settle-intention.text: Judge an intention satisfied or withdrawn. Performed by the steward or the operator, never by a record completing.

intention-operation-set.text: The operations on an intention are: file (anyone), claim and reassess (steward), create a linked record (steward only), send to the desk (steward for intentions, orchestrator for execution questions), answer at the desk (operator), settle (steward or operator). No operation on an intention belongs to the orchestrator or a worker except the orchestrator's direct desk question.

case-triage-desk-discuss.text: Prior art for discussion, in the live triage store (contracts/internal/morphisms/contract.mor, dimension journey): the sorter puts a record on the desk with a static packet of one to four numbered options, a recommendation, and the proposition being judged; a standing ruling can route past the desk. session-2026-09-16-claimability.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim excerpts: "a single intention could create multiple desk items. I was thinking that the intention itself was coming onto my desk, and that's not actually correct." "An intention is never claimable by the operator; only a desk item is. A record is never claimable by an operator, only a worker. ... a pair, record, worker, is claimable by the orchestrator. And yes, a desk item is claimable only by me." "An intention is only claimable by the steward." "the orchestrator can create a desk item ... Is a question just a desk item?" "Whenever it files a question in the agent thread, the system automatically mirrors it in the desk. I can answer it either in the desk or in the agent thread; wherever I answer it, it disappears from both."

desk-item.text: An item on the operator's desk: a question or a proposal with options, linked to the record it concerns and through it to the intention. Birthed by the steward or the orchestrator, or mirrored by the system from an agent-thread question. Claimable only by the operator.

run.text: One worker's turn on a record: the pair (record, worker). Claimable only by the orchestrator, which starts it and owns its outcome, including a blocked return.

one-actor-one-item-kind.text: Each actor claims exactly one kind of item and no other: the steward claims intentions, the orchestrator claims runs, the worker claims records, the operator claims desk items. Any actor's judgment may birth items of another kind, but claiming is exclusive. An intention can birth many records and many desk items.

thread-question-mirrors-to-desk.text: An orchestrator's question in the agent thread is a desk item. The system mirrors it onto the desk without the orchestrator knowing about the desk; the operator may answer in either place, and the answer clears it from both.

session-2026-09-16-ladder.text: Blake, 2026-09-16, verbatim excerpts: "there is this relation which is essentially all about trying to get an intention realised. at each stage something can obstruct this process." "perhaps it's better to think about obstructions to the claimee? steward obs -> desk (resolver=operator) ... worker obs -> flag (resolver=contract auditor)" "Of course this needs to be finite, otherwise we regress." "two types of edges: births/is an attempt at, versus blocked." "i like the idea of the operator being the terminal; makes sense." "a flag is a representation of an obstruction that arose during the attempted manifestation of an intention." "I don't want contract improvements themselves to be treated as a record." "That's the tagline: add it to morphisms. Whatever it is ... is meant to be an intention." On the conflicting-records case: "If it's obstructed, it's obstructed on what? On both of them, right? So do we have many intentions linked to one desk item?" On delegates: "yes, that's pretty good."

worker-role.text: The agent role that performs one run: a contract-governed turn on a record at a node. Constrained by packet, schema and legal edges.

auditor-role.text: The agent role that resolves flags: it rules on whether and how the contract should change. Acts on the frame, not the ladder.

flag.text: An obstruction that arose during an attempt and says the contract itself is the problem. Resolver: the auditor. Not tooling or environment blockage (session 1 F3).

contract.text: The frame an attempt runs under: stores, dimensions, states, edges, schemas, personas. Not a rung on the ladder; changing it is not an attempt at an intention.

start-run.text: The orchestrator starts a worker on a record at a node. Births a run.

return-run.text: The worker ends its run with an outcome: done, or blocked with reason and evidence. Rest of a run wakes the orchestrator.

raise-obstruction.text: An obstructed actor raises an obstruction off the ladder: a desk item (resolver operator) or a flag (resolver auditor). It names the rungs it is about and which of them are frozen while it is open.

rule-on-flag.text: The auditor resolves a flag: rules whether the contract changes. The change itself is frame work by the contract writer, not a record.

operator-is-terminal-resolver.text: Every obstruction has a resolver, and every resolver chain ends at the operator: worker to orchestrator, orchestrator and steward to the operator, worker-about-the-contract to the auditor, auditor to the operator. The operator is the only actor with no resolver. This is what makes the obstruction structure finite.

flag-is-an-obstruction.text: A flag is the representation of an obstruction that arose during the attempted manifestation of an intention, and says the contract is the problem. Its resolver is the auditor.

contract-changes-are-not-records.text: Contract improvements are not records and are not treated as attempts at an intention. They are changes to the frame, made by the contract writer under the operator or after an auditor ruling.

everything-enters-as-intention.text: The user story is one sentence: add it to Morphisms. Whatever enters (a bug, a question, a feature, an idea, a PR) enters as an intention. Records, runs, desk items and flags are all derived from intentions.

obstruction-links-many-rungs.text: An obstruction is off the ladder and points at whatever it stopped: one or many records, across one or many intentions. Its fields are who raised it, who resolves it, which rungs it is about, and which of those are frozen while it is open. These are fields, not kinds.

attempt-ladder.text: One relation, 'is one attempt at', repeated: a record is one attempt at an intention; a run is one attempt at a record's node. Claimed by steward, orchestrator, worker respectively. When a rung comes to rest, the claimer one rung up is woken: run rest wakes the orchestrator, record rest wakes the steward. Note: on the ladder the orchestrator claims the record and the worker claims the run; Blake's phrasing was 'the (record, worker) pair is claimable by the orchestrator', the same fact seen from the run.

attempt-obstruction-dual.text: Two shapes cover everything that happens to an intention: it moves (an attempt: record, run) or it stops (an obstruction: desk item, flag). Attempts go down the ladder, are born from the claimer above, are claimed by a doer, rest when the walk ends, and wake the claimer above. Obstructions go sideways, are born from the obstructed claimer, are claimed by a resolver, rest when answered, and wake the raiser. Fundamental objects: intention, attempt, obstruction.

contract-is-the-frame.text: The contract is the frame the ladder runs under, not a rung. A flag is the one place the ladder points at the frame. Blake: 'getting better, hasn't fully clicked'.

delegates-are-co-seats.text: The assistant and the architect are not actors. They are the operator with a co-seat on one of the operator's own items: the assistant on a desk item for hours, the architect on an intention the operator has taken (the dials route architecture decisions to the desk) for weeks. A design session is the operator stewarding one intention with a co-seat; the theory graph is that seat's ledger. Any user-defined agent has three coordinates: which operator item it shares, how it is driven, how long it lives. Blake: 'yes, that's pretty good'.

running-policy-separates-delegates.text: What separates the contract writer, assistant and architect from an ordinary worker is only the running policy P = (start, drive): the operator drives them turn by turn. Nothing about what they claim differs.
